lesson.title: Atomic Mass: Weighing a Single Atom
lesson.summary: Atomic mass is the measured mass of one specific atom, expressed in atomic mass units defined against a carbon-12 standard.
lesson.body:
Mass number gives a whole-number count of protons plus neutrons, but it is not the same thing as the actual measured mass of an atom. Atomic mass is that measured quantity, expressed in atomic mass units, abbreviated u or sometimes amu. One atomic mass unit is defined as exactly 1/12th the mass of a single, unbound, ground-state carbon-12 atom, which places carbon-12's atomic mass at exactly 12 u by definition. In more familiar units, 1 atomic mass unit equals about 1.6605 times 10 to the negative 27 kilograms, an almost unimaginably small unit chosen specifically because ordinary metric units like kilograms are far too large to conveniently describe single atoms.

If mass number is just a particle count, why is atomic mass not simply equal to mass number? The answer lies in nuclear binding energy. When protons and neutrons bind together into a nucleus, a small amount of mass is converted into the energy that holds the nucleus together, following Einstein's mass-energy relationship. This means the true measured mass of a nucleus is always slightly less than the sum of the masses of its separate protons and neutrons. For most isotopes this effect shifts atomic mass just slightly away from a whole number equal to the mass number, which is why atomic mass values carry decimal places even for a single, pure isotope.

A worked example makes the distinction concrete. Carbon-12 has a mass number of 12, and by the very definition of the atomic mass unit, its atomic mass is set at exactly 12.000 u. Carbon-13, however, has a mass number of 13, but its measured atomic mass is 13.00335 u, not exactly 13. That small excess above the whole number reflects the actual measured mass of a carbon-13 nucleus's protons, neutrons, and binding energy together, determined experimentally using instruments such as a mass spectrometer, which measures atomic masses with remarkable precision by tracking how ions of different mass behave in electric and magnetic fields.

It helps to also compare atomic mass to the actual masses of the particles involved. A single proton has a mass of about 1.007276 u, and a single neutron has a mass of about 1.008665 u. Adding six protons and six neutrons gives 6 times 1.007276, plus 6 times 1.008665, equal to 6.043656 plus 6.05199, or about 12.095646 u, noticeably more than carbon-12's actual atomic mass of exactly 12 u. That roughly 0.096 u difference is the mass converted into nuclear binding energy holding carbon-12's nucleus together, a small but real and measurable effect.

Atomic mass, as defined here, describes one specific isotope's measured mass, whether that is carbon-12 at exactly 12 u or carbon-13 at 13.00335 u. But most elements exist in nature as a mixture of multiple isotopes at fixed proportions, and the periodic table does not list the atomic mass of any single isotope. Instead it lists a weighted blend across all naturally occurring isotopes, a quantity called average atomic mass, which combines the atomic mass of each isotope with how abundant that isotope actually is in nature.
